OMG
OH-em-JEE
interjection (Millennial slang)
Initialism for Oh my God. Its first known written use is a 1917 letter from Admiral John Fisher to Winston Churchill ("O.M.G. (Oh! My God!)"), but the modern life began in 1990s chat rooms and exploded with 2000s texting. Millennials used it as a reflex for any surprise, delight, or outrage ("OMG I can’t," "OMG Becky"), and it moved from screens to speech, spoken as letters. The Oxford English Dictionary added it in 2011. Variants: OMFG (vulgar), OMGosh, omw is unrelated ("on my way").

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

OMG is "Oh my God" reduced to three letters and spent on everything: a sale, a celebrity, a cute dog, a bad grade. It is the most common use of the divine name in the Millennial vocabulary, and almost never a prayer. The Christian observation must be direct, because the commandment is: "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain" (Exo 20:7). To take His name in vain is to lift it up emptily, to use it for no purpose, as filler or exclamation. The abbreviation does not change what is being said; it only makes it easier to say without noticing. The first petition of the Lord’s Prayer asks the opposite: "Hallowed be thy name" (Mat 6:9). "Holy and reverend is his name" (Psa 111:9). There is a right way to say these very words. When Thomas saw the risen Christ and touched His wounds, he said, "My Lord and my God" (Joh 20:28), and it was the truest confession in the Gospels. A father teaches his children both lessons at once: never spend God’s name on a pair of shoes, and always be ready to say it, with your whole heart, about Jesus Christ. Give them other words for surprise; there are hundreds.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial initialism (1990s chat, 2000s texting; OED 2011) for Oh my God as a reflex exclamation; the divine name spent as filler, which the third commandment forbids (Exo 20:7). Reject.

OMG, interj. (Millennial text and speech slang, 1990s–present; initialism of Oh my God) An exclamation of surprise, excitement, or dismay, applied to anything. Spoken as letters: "Oh-em-gee." Vulgar intensive: OMFG.

First recorded 1917 (Admiral Fisher to Churchill); mainstream with 2000s texting; Oxford English Dictionary 2011.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:7 — "Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain."

Mat 6:9 — "After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name."

Psa 111:9 — "He sent redemption unto his people: he hath commanded his covenant for ever: holy and reverend is his name."

Joh 20:28 — "And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God."

Lev 22:32 — "Neither shall ye profane my holy name; but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel: I am the LORD which hallow you,"

Modern Corruption

OMG spends the name of God as filler for every surprise; the third commandment forbids taking His name in vain, and the abbreviation only makes the sin easier to miss.

expand to see more

The corruption is the cheapening of the holiest word a mouth can say. Israel was commanded, "Neither shall ye profane my holy name; but I will be hallowed among the children of Israel" (Lev 22:32), and Jews of the Second Temple period feared misusing the Name so much that they stopped pronouncing it at all. Our culture has moved to the opposite pole: the Name is so constant in exclamation that it no longer registers as His. A child raised on OMG learns, without anyone teaching it, that God is a word one says when a cake looks good.

The recovery is not prudishness but reverence and readiness. The same three words are the summit of Christian confession on Thomas’s lips. Teach the young to guard the Name in casual speech and to hallow it in prayer; to substitute honest exclamations for the reflex; and, when they meet the risen Christ in His Word, to say "My Lord and my God" and mean every syllable. A tongue trained to reverence will not waste the Name, and will not be ashamed of it either.
